ca_cyclops_rock.blurb: Cyclops Rock is a compact, flat-topped monzogranite formation in the Hidden Valley area of Joshua Tree, just east of the campground. A hole high on the rock gives it its name and makes it easy to spot. Most of the 28 climbs are traditional crack and face lines, with a handful of top-ropes and a lone bolted route. Grades run from easy fifth class through the 5.11s, with a scattering at 5.12, so there is something for beginners and for stronger climbers. A short walk from the parking area puts you at the base, which suits a quick morning or an afternoon between other formations.

ca_3_southeast_face.blurb: The Southeast Face is one of the two great walls of El Capitan, the granite monolith on the north side of Yosemite Valley. It is a big-wall destination: routes here run from roughly seven to over thirty pitches, and nearly all of the 28 climbs are aid or aid-with-free-climbing lines, mostly in the A3 to A4 range. A few free lines reach into the high 5.13s and 5.14. Expect multi-day ascents with hauling, a full wall rack and real commitment. This is a place for experienced wall climbers, with long, sustained days on pale, steep, largely unbroken granite.

ca_tower_two_area.blurb: Tower Two is a small pocket of granodiorite on Mount Woodson, the boulder-strewn peak in northern San Diego County that locals rate as the county's best bouldering. The 28 climbs are a mixed bag: roughly sixteen boulder problems from V0 to V10 and beyond, nine short trad lines and a few top-ropes up to the 5.11s. The rock has a Joshua Tree feel, and several of the short routes share a single anchor, which makes it handy for a quick session. The walk in is brief. It gets hot in summer, so spring, autumn and early mornings are the comfortable times.

ca_dome_the.blurb: The Dome is the largest section of Split Rock, in the Cold Springs climbing area of northwest California. This dome-shaped block stands about 30 to 50 feet tall, and its sides differ: the north is short and steep, the west is smooth and overhanging, and the southeast is low-angle and well featured. Most of the 28 climbs are bolted sport routes, with a few top-ropes and boulder problems. Grades start at easy fifth class and cluster in the 5.11s, with some at 5.12 and 5.13 and a couple of hard V7 and V8 problems. Trails through woods and small meadows lead to the base in just a few minutes.

ca_snickers_north_face.blurb: The north side of the Snickers formation sits in the Echo Rock area of Joshua Tree. It is mostly a crack-climbing wall, with a few newer bolted lines among 28 routes, split between trad, sport, a top-rope and a single aid line. The rock carries plenty of gray varnish. Grades range from the high 5.7s up to 5.12, with most climbs at 5.10 and 5.11. The big draw is shade: the face turns shady by mid-morning in March and is in shadow most of the day in winter, so it is a smart choice when other walls are baking. Allow roughly ten to fifteen minutes of mostly flat walking from the lot.

ca_dozier_dome.blurb: Dozier Dome is a granodiorite dome in Tuolumne Meadows, tucked next to Medlicott Dome and out of sight of the highway, so it sees modest traffic. The 28 climbs lean traditional, with a handful of sport lines and one top-rope. They combine cracks with bolted knob-studded face climbing, and the grades are friendly: most sit between 5.7 and 5.10, with a few at 5.11 and one easy start below 5.7. It is a good pick for climbers stepping into Tuolumne multi-pitch, with several moderate, enjoyable lines. Reaching the base means a short forest walk and following cairns over granite, so bring a little route-finding patience.

ca_1_northeast_face.blurb: The Northeast Face is the steepest aspect of Calaveras Dome, a granite dome reached from Highway 88 near Carson Pass in the Stanislaus National Forest. Routes here are long, with climbs reaching up to about 1,200 feet, and most of the 27 are traditional multi-pitch lines of splitter cracks, corners and demanding face moves, plus a few bolted routes. Grades start at 5.9, but the bulk fall at 5.11 and 5.12, so it suits experienced leaders. Morning sun reaches the face first, and it is usually in shade by the middle of the afternoon. Two ropes will get you down most lines by rappel, and the trail to the base is faint but obvious.
